newsitem.title: UK: Major's Conservatives come back in opinion polls.
newsitem.headline: Major's Conservatives come back in opinion polls.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives have slashed the opinion poll lead of the Labour opposition to 17 points and Labour's support is at its lowest level since Tony Blair became leader in July 1994, a poll showed on Thursday.
The MORI poll of 1,515 adults showed Labour's support at 50 percent, the Conservatives at 33 percent -- its highest level since early 1993 -- and the centrist Liberal Democrats at 12 percent.
The last MORI poll two weeks ago had Labour's lead at 28 points and their rating among voters at 56 points. An election must be held by May 1997.
Dissatisfaction with Prime Minister John Major's government had declined as evidence of economic well-being -- the so-called feelgood factor -- has grown among Britain's 44 million voters.

But Labour's lead is still historically very high so close to an election. Six months before the 1992 election, Labour held a two-point lead, MORI said. Under Blair, the party has moved steadily to the centre ground of British politics.

Three other recent opinion polls gave Labour leads of 29, 27 and 15 points. Opinion polls show different levels of support according to the questions asked, how polling organisations adjust their raw figures and the numbers of people who decline to state a party preference.
The Conservatives have been in power since 1979.
